---
title: "Open Problems in Target Trial Emulation"
subtitle: "An audited catalog of what is actually unsolved in target trial emulation"
toc: false
---

Target trial emulation gave observational comparative effectiveness research a discipline it
lacked: state the protocol of the randomized trial you would have run, then say exactly how each
component is emulated in the data you have. That discipline removed a class of self-inflicted
errors. It did not remove the rest.

This site catalogs the open problems, one entry at a time. Each says what the problem is, why it
stays open, what has already been tried, and the most probable route to a solution.

## The organizing distinction

The decisive division is between problems a **complete protocol specification solves** and
problems that **survive a perfect protocol**.

Writing the protocol down is what defeats misalignment of eligibility, assignment and the start
of follow-up, and with it immortal time bias. Those problems are, in principle, bookkeeping: they
are caused by the analyst and fixed by the analyst. The catalog records them because applied
practice still gets them wrong, not because the theory is missing.

Everything else survives. A protocol states which confounders you intend to adjust for; it cannot
make them measured. It states a sustained strategy; it cannot make that strategy achievable in
people whose covariate history never receives it. It names an outcome; it cannot make the
phenotype algorithm that ascertains the outcome correct. Most of the hardest entries here sit on
that side of the line.

Three consequences run through the whole collection.

**Emulation prevents self-inflicted bias; it does not create randomization.** An immaculately
aligned time zero and an active-comparator new-user design remove specific, nameable errors. They
leave exchangeability exactly where it was: an assumption, untestable from the data being
analyzed. Covariate balance after weighting is evidence about the variables you measured and
silent about the ones you did not.

**Choices made before any model is fitted cannot be priced by the model.** The grace period, the
time grid, the lookback window, the code list defining the outcome: each is fixed before
estimation, and each changes the estimand rather than merely the precision. No amount of
flexibility in the nuisance models recovers a choice made upstream of them.

**Agreement with a randomized trial is calibration evidence, not certification.** When an
emulation and its index trial disagree, the candidates are residual confounding, a different
population, differently measured exposure or outcome, a different estimand, and chance. Nothing
in the current toolkit separates them for the single study in front of a decision maker.

## Reading a verdict

Every entry carries a verdict recording what happened when its claims were checked against the
literature and against independent external auditors. A verdict of
[Overstated]{.verdict .verdict-overstated} does not mean the problem is not real; it usually means
the underlying issue is real and a claim about its severity was pitched too strongly. Entries
marked [Resolved since report]{.verdict .verdict-resolved-since-report} are kept rather than
deleted, because knowing that something was recently closed is as useful as knowing it is open.

The source material for this catalog was produced by a large language model and then audited.
[How this was verified](methods.qmd) explains what that means in practice, including where the
audit's own limits are.
